Recap of lecture 8: primary-backup replication (VMware fault tolerance paper); the open problem was who decides the primary is dead, since guessing wrong causes split brain; VMware's test-and-set arbiter is itself a single point of failure.
Two-phase commit is not consensus: it needs every participant to vote yes and blocks if the coordinator crashes; consensus makes progress with a majority (answer to Devon's question).

Replicated state machine approach: deterministic state machines on each server applying the same commands in the same order reach the same state, so the problem reduces to keeping a replicated log identical.
Nondeterministic commands (random, clock) must be evaluated once by the leader and the concrete value put in the log entry; consensus does not fix a nondeterministic state machine.
Consensus is hard because servers crash, messages are delayed/dropped/duplicated/reordered, networks partition, and a crashed server cannot be distinguished from a slow one.

FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985): in a fully asynchronous system no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination if even one process can crash; students should be able to state this and how practical systems get around it.
Practical algorithms (Paxos, Raft) sidestep FLP by always guaranteeing safety but guaranteeing progress only when the network behaves reasonably (messages arrive within timeouts).
The proof of FLP will NOT be on the exam (only the statement and its implications).
Safety: nothing bad ever happens (a violation occurs at a finite point); for consensus, two servers never decide different values for the same log slot.
Liveness: something good eventually happens (no finite point of violation); for consensus, a value is eventually decided.

Raft never gives up safety, even under partitions and delays; when the network is bad it gives up liveness (may stall). Safety vs liveness definitions and which Raft guarantees unconditionally will be on the exam.
A quorum is a subset of servers large enough that any two quorums overlap; Raft uses majority quorums, and any two majorities share at least one server, which carries decisions forward.
Majority quorum size is floor(n/2)+1: 3 of 5 servers, 2 of 3 servers.
To tolerate f crash failures you need 2f+1 servers: 3 servers tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2, 7 tolerate 3. The quorum formula and 2f+1 will be on the exam.
A 4-node cluster (majority 3) tolerates only 1 failure, the same as 3 nodes; even-sized clusters never add fault tolerance (6 tolerates 2, same as 5).
facts.notes: explicit correction of the earlier claim that 4 nodes tolerate 2 failures (C02)

facts.statement: Raft comes from the 2014 paper 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm' by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout (Stanford), best paper at USENIX ATC; its primary design goal was understandability.
Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety (plus membership changes and log compaction as add-ons).
Raft uses a strong leader: all client requests go through the leader and log entries flow only from leader to followers; every server is a follower, candidate, or leader.

A term is a monotonically increasing number acting as a logical clock; each term begins with an election and has at most one leader (election safety), and some terms have no leader after a split vote.
A server seeing a higher term updates its term and steps down to follower if it was leader or candidate; requests carrying a lower term are rejected.

Basic Raft needs only two RPCs: RequestVote (candidates, during elections) and AppendEntries (leaders, replicating entries and serving as heartbeat when empty); InstallSnapshot is a third RPC for log compaction.

Leader election: a follower that hears no valid heartbeat within its election timeout increments its term, becomes candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote in parallel; it wins with votes from a majority of the full cluster (3 of 5).
Each server votes for at most one candidate per term (first-come, first-served), which together with majority voting guarantees at most one leader per term.

Persistent state (currentTerm, votedFor, and the log) must be written to stable storage before responding to RPCs; forgetting votedFor can produce two leaders in one term. commitIndex, lastApplied, nextIndex and matchIndex are volatile.
Raft uses randomized election timeouts, chosen fresh on each reset from a fixed interval; the paper uses 150-300 milliseconds, which makes split votes rare.
RequestVote arguments are term, candidateId, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm; the reply contains term and voteGranted.
Answering Jordan's question on fixed priorities: the Raft authors first tried a ranking system but hit subtle availability corner cases, so they chose randomized timeouts as simpler to reason about.
Raft's safety never depends on timing but liveness does: broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF (roughly 0.5-20ms, 10-500ms, and months).
The homework tester allows at most 10 heartbeats per second per server and requires a new leader to be elected within 5 seconds of the old leader failing.
For the homework, the recommended randomized election timeout is about 400-800ms, larger than the paper's 150-300ms, because of the tester's heartbeat limit.
Reset the election timer only when granting a vote or receiving a valid AppendEntries from the current leader, not on every RequestVote; the #1 homework 4 bug is holding a lock while sending an RPC.
Split vote example: in term 6 leader A crashes; B (212ms) and D (213ms) both run in term 7 and get 2 votes each so term 7 has no leader; D then times out first (160ms) and wins term 8 with 3 votes.

War story: at payments startup Ledgerline in 2017, the professor's team moved an etcd-based config store from 3 nodes to 4 split 2 in Virginia and 2 in Ohio; when the inter-site link flapped neither side had a majority and the store was unavailable for 47 minutes, queuing about 38,000 payment authorizations (no data lost).
To survive losing a whole data center you need three sites, e.g. 2+2+1 = 5 nodes; Ledgerline did this the next quarter at the cost of higher write latency.

Each log entry has a command, the term when the leader received it, and an index (starting at 1). AppendEntries carries term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries, and leaderCommit; followers reject it if they lack a matching entry at prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm (the consistency check).
Log matching property: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical in all entries up through that index (proved by induction via the consistency check).

The leader repairs inconsistent followers by forcing their logs to match its own: it tracks nextIndex per follower (initialized past its last entry), decrements it on rejection, and tracks matchIndex for commitment; homework 5's backup test needs the skip-by-conflicting-term optimization.

Commit index: the highest log index a server knows to be committed (starts at 0, only increases); the leader sends it as leaderCommit and followers set theirs to min(leaderCommit, index of last new entry); lastApplied tracks what has been applied to the state machine.
Committed is a cluster-wide fact (durable, never lost); applied is per server (executed against its local state machine).

Worked example (5 servers, term 3, leader A): logs by term are A and B 1,1,2,3,3,3; C and E 1,1,2,3,3; D 1,1,2. Index 5 is on 4 of 5 servers so A's commit index is 5; index 6 is only on A and B and is uncommitted.

After A crashes: D times out first (155ms), runs in term 4, and is rejected by all (its last log term 2 is older); C times out (170ms), runs in term 5, is rejected by B (same last term, B's log longer) but wins with votes from C, D and E; C's new term-5 entry at index 6 overwrites B's uncommitted term-3 entry.

Election restriction: a voter denies its vote if its own log is more up-to-date than the candidate's; up-to-date is compared by the term of the last entry first, and only if equal by log length (so the longest log does not automatically win).
A log with 5 entries ending in term 3 is more up-to-date than a log with 7 entries ending in term 2.

Leader completeness property: if an entry is committed in a given term, it is present in the logs of the leaders of all higher-numbered terms (because the committing majority and the electing majority overlap).

The election restriction, the up-to-date comparison, and leader completeness will be on the exam, likely as a 'given five logs, which servers can become leader' question (not the lecture's exact example).

Commitment rule: a leader only commits entries from its current term by counting replicas; entries from earlier terms are committed indirectly once a current-term entry after them is committed (via log matching).

Figure 8 scenario (Devon's question): an index-2 term-2 entry replicated to a majority (A, B, C) by leader A in term 4 can still be overwritten when E, holding a term-3 entry, wins term 5; it is safe only after A commits a term-4 entry at index 3 on a majority.
The current-term commitment rule and the Figure 8 scenario will be on the exam ('I promise'); many students lose points writing 'committed once on a majority'.
A new leader appends a no-op entry at the start of its term to commit a current-term entry quickly (paper section 8).

Partition scenario: 5 servers with leader B in term 7 and commit index 20 are split into a minority {A, B} and a majority {C, D, E}; B appends client 1's 'set x to 7' at index 21 but reaches only 2 of 5 servers, so it cannot commit it or reply to the client.
In the partition scenario, on the majority side E times out first (210ms), wins term 8 with votes from C and D, and commits client 2's 'set y to 3' at index 21.

During a partition two leaders can coexist only in different terms, and the older-term leader cannot commit, so safety holds; on healing B sees term 8, steps down, and its uncommitted index-21 entry is overwritten.

Answering Jordan's question: the unacknowledged write is not lost from Raft's perspective; the client times out and retries at the new leader, and clients attach a unique client ID and per-command serial number so the state machine deduplicates retries and each command takes effect exactly once.

A stale leader can serve stale reads; the fix is for the leader to confirm leadership by exchanging heartbeats with a majority before answering reads (etcd's ReadIndex), or to use leases, which depend on bounded clock drift.

An isolated server keeps incrementing its term (e.g. to 12) and on rejoining forces a healthy leader to step down; pre-vote (from Ongaro's dissertation, implemented by etcd) prevents this by asking for hypothetical votes before bumping the term.

Switching cluster configuration directly is unsafe: going from 3 servers to 5, old-config and new-config majorities (e.g. A,B and C,D,E) can elect two leaders in the same term because the majorities do not overlap.

Joint consensus: the leader commits a C-old,new entry during which decisions need separate majorities of both configurations, then commits C-new; new servers join as non-voting learners first, and many implementations instead use single-server changes.
For the exam, students need to know why configurations cannot be switched directly, but not the step-by-step joint consensus protocol.

Paxos is Leslie Lamport's algorithm ('The Part-Time Parliament', written around 1990, published 1998; 'Paxos Made Simple', 2001); basic Paxos runs prepare/promise and accept/accepted phases with majorities, and Multi-Paxos runs one instance per log slot with a stable leader.

Raft is close to a well-specified Multi-Paxos with a strong leader: its log has no holes, a new leader already has all committed entries, and it is a complete specification; fault tolerance (2f+1) and normal-case performance are the same.

Raft is not strictly better than Paxos: the strong leader is a write bottleneck, variants like EPaxos can do better for geo-distributed low-conflict workloads, and easier to understand does not mean faster or more available.

etcd uses Raft and backs Kubernetes cluster state; it recommends 3 or 5 members (discouraging much beyond 7) and defaults to a 100ms heartbeat and 1000ms election timeout. Caveat: using its locks safely requires fencing tokens because leases can expire during client pauses.

Consul (HashiCorp) runs Raft only on its 3 or 5 server nodes via HashiCorp's Raft library; client agents are not voters (membership via gossip), and its default read mode relies on leader leasing and can briefly return stale data.

CockroachDB splits data into ranges, each its own Raft group usually with 3 replicas (Multi-Raft, with coalesced heartbeats); reads go through leaseholders and cross-range transactions need a separate commit protocol on top of Raft.
Google's Chubby and Spanner use Paxos; ZooKeeper uses its own protocol, Zab.

'Uses Raft' does not mean a system is correct: implementations add pre-vote, check-quorum, leases, batching, and snapshots, and Jepsen analyses have found bugs usually in the code around the algorithm.

Log compaction via snapshots: each server independently snapshots its committed state and discards log entries up to the last included index, storing last included index and term (for the consistency check) and the latest configuration; the leader sends InstallSnapshot to followers too far behind. This is homework 6.
